newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS-Wheat importers mark time as prices tumble.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Wheat importers mark time as prices tumble.

text.p: Sliding world wheat prices have failed to trigger widespread buying from importing nations, leaving markets looking shaky as harvest time approaches in the northern hemisphere, European grain traders said on Wednesday.
Benchmark July Chicago futures started out fragile again on Wednesday after losing three percent the previous day when funds dumped the contract on improved crop hopes in the United States.
In early business July fell 5-1/2 cents to a three-month low of $3.58 a bushel. It has been falling steadily since peaking at $4.50 in April during a frost damage scare that later receded.
Some analysts now set their sights on $3.50 a bushel, though technical charts suggest a few upward blips on the way.
"There is little demand right now and many buyers are covered through July. They are not in a hurry," one trader said.
Wednesday brought fresh evidence of that with private Egyptian firms launching a tender to buy 100,000 tonnes of wheat, but only for delivery between August and October.
Egypt has been virtually alone in snapping up wheat from Australia, America and others in recent weeks.
But unlike last year when importers competed for every last bushel in store right up to the new harvest, most seem happy to wait out the gap between crop cycles and watch prices crumple.
Algeria, Morocco and Tunisia are among countries said to be checking prices without making a move, while a record buying spree from Iran also seems to have paused at least for now.
The lower U.S. prices already translate into wheat on the world market around $135 a tonne, far below records of almost twice that seen in April last year when stocks were low.
"There is more surplus around generally and buyers are feeling more comfortable," a European trader said.
A big factor driving wheat downwards has been a bail-out of speculative positions built up on reports of significant damage to the U.S. hard red winter crop when a freeze hit in April.

"In fact weather conditions since the freeze have been nothing short of ideal, leaving the market wondering how much damage will actually be evident when final yields come in," London-based brokerage GNI Ltd said in a report.
Prices have also shrugged off a clampdown on exports by the European Union, a key supplier behind the U.S. and Canada, and now seen likely to stay off the market for a month.

An EU source said on Wednesday the 15-nation bloc would not start selling ahead from this year's harvest until at least late June, a month later than usual. And a rare export tax designed to control domestic prices stays in place for the time being.
Nonetheless a recovery from drought is fuelling hopes of a good EU crop and may soon put extra pressure on Brussels to resume exporting with subsidies, despite U.S. opposition.

Some traders cautioned wheat could still snap higher if importers come out in a block to buy as prices stabilise. But most expect the market will find it harder to rally unless the weather really turns foul. And the days of huge buying by Russia and China remain buried by financial woes or good Chinese crops.
